name: Trophimus
source_summary: An Ephesian believer who traveled with Paul, whose presence with Paul in Jerusalem sparked a riot when Jews mistakenly assumed Paul had brought him, a Gentile, into the temple's restricted area, and whom Paul later left behind at Miletus due to illness.
family_friendly_summary: Trophimus was a believer from Ephesus who traveled together with Paul on his journeys, part of a group carrying gifts collected for the believers in Jerusalem. While in Jerusalem, some people saw Trophimus, who was a Gentile, in the city with Paul and wrongly assumed Paul had brought him into a restricted area of the temple that only Jewish people were allowed to enter. This false assumption caused a huge uproar and led directly to Paul's arrest. Later, in one of Paul's final letters, he mentions leaving Trophimus behind at Miletus because he was sick. Trophimus's story shows how a simple misunderstanding could spiral into a major, dangerous situation for someone serving faithfully alongside Paul.
adult_story: Trophimus, from Ephesus, is named among the group of men from various churches who accompanied Paul on his journey carrying the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem (Acts 20:4). His presence with Paul in Jerusalem became the spark for one of the most consequential moments in Paul's ministry: some Jews from Asia, having previously seen Trophimus, a Gentile, together with Paul in the city, spotted Paul in the temple and wrongly assumed he had brought Trophimus into the inner court reserved exclusively for Jews, a serious violation punishable by death (Acts 21:27-29). Though the accusation was factually mistaken -- Paul had not actually brought Trophimus into the restricted area -- the crowd's outrage stirred the whole city, and Paul was seized, beaten, and would have been killed had Roman soldiers not intervened, an arrest that led directly to his years of imprisonment and eventual journey to Rome (21:30-36). Trophimus himself is not recorded as being harmed in the incident, and appears once more, near the end of Paul's ministry: in his final letter to Timothy, Paul mentions plainly, 'Trophimus I left sick at Miletus' (2 Timothy 4:20), a small, human detail showing that not even Paul's own traveling companions were exempt from ordinary illness or the practical limits it placed on continued travel and ministry together.
christ_connections: The riot ignited by the false assumption Paul had brought Trophimus, a Gentile, past the temple's dividing wall is a striking real-world collision with exactly the barrier Paul describes Christ having torn down: 'He Himself is our peace... and broke down the barrier of the dividing wall' (Ephesians 2:14) -- a truth Paul carried toward Jerusalem even as the city violently resisted living by it.

Trophimus's illness, mentioned in one of Paul's last letters, is a small reminder that gospel work continues through ordinary human weakness and limitation, the same pattern Paul says displays Christ's power made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9).
